tench: Tench are typically a dark green or olive color, blending into their preferred muddy habitats.
The body of the tench is thick and cylindrical, and it's covered in small, embedded scales.
A defining feature of the tench is its pair of barbels, whisker-like sensory organs, located on either side of the mouth.
The dorsal fin of the tench is set far back on the body, with the rounded pelvic and pectoral fins often a red or orange color.
The tail fin of the tench is slightly forked and rounded, aiding in its slow, steady movement.
Tench typically grow to around 50-70 cm in length, with some specimens reaching up to 90 cm.
Tench have small, dark eyes that are slightly downturned, giving them a subdued appearance.
goldfish: Goldfish are known for their bright orange or gold color, but they can also come in other colors like white, black, red, and yellow.
Goldfish have different shapes depending on their type, ranging from slender to more egg-shaped varieties.
Comparatively, goldfish are generally smaller than many other objects that may appear in the image.
Goldfish either have a single dorsal fin or multiple fins depending on their variety, along with paired pectoral and pelvic fins, and a forked caudal (tail) fin.
The scales of a goldfish are typically shiny and metallic, but some varieties have unique textured scales.
Goldfish vary in size, with some types growing up to 12 inches in length while others are significantly smaller.
Some varieties of goldfish have special eye shapes, such as the telescope goldfish with its bulging eyes or the bubble eye goldfish with fluid-filled sacs underneath its eyes.
great white shark: Great white sharks are known for their slate-grey upper bodies to blend in with the rocky sea floor, while their bellies are white.
The great white shark is characterized by its conical snout. The snout shape allows efficient flow of water into the shark's mouth for oxygen and makes it powerful to prey on.
They have a streamlined torpedo-shaped body, making them an exceptional swimmer.
The relative size of a great white shark is large compared to other objects in the image.
Great white sharks have large, triangular, serrated teeth suitable for ripping into the flesh of their prey.
The great white shark has a distinctive dorsal fin that acts as a stabilizer when the shark swims.
Great white sharks have a unique attribute called countershading: they can change their color shades between the top and bottom of their bodies for camouflage in different water depths.
tiger shark: Tiger sharks are known for their distinctive dark stripes on a lighter gray or blue background, similar to the pattern seen on tigers.
Tiger sharks have a unique nose shape that is blunt and rounded, unlike many other shark species that have a more pointed snout.
Tiger sharks are large in size, typically measuring between 10 and 14 feet in length, though they can grow even larger.
Tiger sharks have a robust, bulky body with a flat and wide head, and a tail with a long upper lobe.
Tiger sharks have an array of sharp, highly serrated teeth that are perfectly designed for shearing through flesh and bone.

The dorsal side of a tiger shark is darker in color which provides excellent camouflage when viewed from above, while the underside is lighter to blend in with brighter surface waters when viewed from below.
Tiger sharks are known for their aggressive and opportunistic feeding behavior, predating on a wide variety of organisms.
hammerhead shark: Hammerhead sharks are known for their unique head shape, which is flattened and extended into a 'hammer' shape called a cephalofoil.
The eyes of hammerhead sharks are located on the ends of the 'hammer', providing a 360-degree field of vision.
Hammerhead sharks have a grayish-brown to olive-green color on the top part of their body, with a lighter underside to camouflage them from predators and prey.
They have a tall triangular dorsal fin, and a sickle-shaped caudal (tail) fin with a distinct notch on the upper part.
Relative to other objects in the image, hammerhead sharks can be quite large, with some species growing up to 20 feet in length.
Hammerhead sharks typically swim in the open ocean, indicating a marine environment in the background.
Hammerhead sharks have a row of sharp, polygonal teeth that are designed for catching and eating prey, including fish, squid, and octopus.
electric ray: Electric rays are known for their flat, circular or heart-shaped bodies, which are covered in smooth skin.
They are typically dark gray, brown, or black on top with a white or lighter-colored belly.
Electric rays have two large, rounded pectoral fins that form a disk around its body, and a short tail with a small dorsal fin and a rounded caudal(fin) fin.
The eyes and spiracles (breathing openings) can be found on the top of the body, while the mouth and gill slits are located on the underside of the body.
One of the most distinct features of electric rays is the presence of electric organs located on each side of the head, which are used for defense and hunting.
Sometimes, two small dorsal fins can be seen towards the end of its tail.
Electric rays are bottom dwellers and are often seen partially buried in sand or mud with only their eyes and spiracles visible.
stingray: Stingrays are recognized for their flat, diamond or round shaped bodies, which help them camouflage on the seafloor.
Stingrays possess long, whip-like tails that often have one or more sharp, venomous barbs, which they use for self-defense.
The color of stingrays usually varies from olive to green, brown, grey or black on the top surface, and pale or white underside.
Stingrays have small, round eyes on the top of their body and gills on the undersides.
In terms of size, stingrays can range from a small as a dinner plate to as large as several feet in diameter.
Stingrays are usually found on the seafloor, often partially buried in sand.
Some species of Stingrays, like the manta ray, are known for their 'wings', which they flap in a bird-like manner to swim.
rooster: A male chicken known for its vibrant plumage, prominent comb, and loud crowing at dawn. It often serves as a symbol of vigilance and morning.
Roosters are typically larger and more strikingly colored than hens, often displaying a variety of hues like red, blue, green, gold, and black in their feathers.
One of the most distinctive features of a rooster is its large, bright red or flesh-colored comb on top of the head and wattles hanging below the chin.
Roosters have a louder crow than hens, and they typically crow to claim their territory, especially in the early morning.
Roosters have a strong and upright posture, with a broad chest and muscular build.
Their legs are strong with long, curved claws, adapted to scratching the ground in search of food.
Roosters display iridescent feathers often with a metallic sheen, especially at their tails.
hen: Hens are domesticated birds, they have a round body draped with feathers in various colors such as red, white, black, or mixes.
Hens have a distinctively shaped beak, short and curved downwards, used for pecking food.
Hens have a red comb on top of their head and two earlobes hanging on either side.
The relative size of hens is larger compared to smaller birds but smaller than most domesticated animals.
They have thick bone legs ending in three pointed toes and are covered in scales.
Hens lay eggs, and are often pictured near nests filled with light brown or white eggs.
Some breeds of hens can have a fan-shaped tail, especially prominent in roosters.
ostrich: Ostriches are large, flightless birds which are distinguished by their long, thin necks and legs.
They are known for their large, round bodies covered with black and white feathers.
An ostrich's head is relatively small in comparison to its body, with large eyes and a long, flat beak.
Ostriches have two large, strong toes on each foot, which they use for running at high speeds.
They are known for their ability to run fast, being the fastest bird on land with a top speed of about 60 mph.
Ostriches have large, prominent eyes, which are said to be bigger than any other land animal's.
They are the tallest birds in the world, with males growing up to 9 feet tall.
brambling: Bramblings have a strong white wing bar, contrasting black flight feathers and orange-red body.
In winter, bramblings have a white belly and dark, streaked flanks.
The size of a brambling can be relative to other objects in the image, but they typically measure around 14 to 16 cm in length.
The adult male in summer has a solid black head, back and throat, with a white rump and largely white belly with reddish vent.
The females and young bramblings have more subtle yellow-buff tones and a pink flush to the underparts.
Bramblings have a robust, conical bill which is yellow in winter and darker, blackish-brown during summer.
The bramble's tail is forked and noticeably long when the bird is in flight.
goldfinch: Goldfinches are known for their bright yellow feathers during the breeding season, especially males. They may turn a more muted yellow-brown during the winter.
Goldfinches have a distinctive flight pattern, alternating bouts of flapping with periods of gliding, which is often noticeable in images.
Goldfinches have a slim, pointed beak that helps them extract seeds from thistle plants, their primary food source.
The relative size of Goldfinches is smaller compared to other birds in the image.
Goldfinches have black wings with a broad, white stripe, and a black tail with white spots.
Male goldfinches are more brightly colored, while females tend to have more muted tones.
During the breeding season, males have a conspicuous bright red face, while females have a more subdued face color.
house finch: These birds are small-bodied, around the size of a sparrow, so in a photo they would appear small in comparison to other elements.
House finches have a distinctive red or rosy coloration on their head, breast, and rump with brown streaked back and wings.
The females are brown and streaked overall, they do not have the rosy coloration like the males.
House finches have square-tipped brown tails and wings with distinctive stripes.
Their bills are short and deep, ideal for their diet which consists mainly of seeds, berries and fruits.
The eye region is surrounded by a plain, unmarked face, with a slight curve in the brow giving them a frowning appearance.
These birds are often found in urban or suburban areas and are likely to be seen in man-made structures or trees.
junco: Juncos are generally small, grayish birds with a pink bill and white outer tail feathers that flash distinctively in flight.
The size of the junco is generally small when compared to other objects in the image, usually measuring between 5.5 to 6.3 inches in length.
Juncos have a round body with a fairly long, pointed beak, which is handy for their seed-based diet.
Juncos are usually slate colored or dark gray, often with a lighter chest. However, the colors can vary between different species.
Juncos often inhabit areas with coniferous trees or mixed woodlands, so images of juncos may also include these types of environments in the background.
The habitat of a junco can range from forests to suburban areas, and they are often sighted hopping on the ground or perching on low branches.
Juncos are known for their distinctive chirping call, but this auditory attribute may be hard to capture in an image.
indigo bunting: The indigo bunting is a small bird, measuring around five to six inches in length. Relative size in the image may help with identification if other objects provide a reference point.
The adult male indigo bunting is a vibrant blue, which may appear purple in certain lighting conditions. This brilliant color is a distinctive identifying characteristic.
Female and juvenile indigo buntings have a much less conspicuous appearance, being primarily brown with a hint of blue on the wings and tail.
This songbird has a small, conical beak suited to its diet of seeds and grains. The shape and size of its beak can help in identifying this bird.
Indigo buntings, like many birds, have sharp, pointed wings and a notched tail.
They are often seen in open areas with low vegetation, perched at the tops of trees or on telephone wires. Their habitat and behavior can provide context for identification.
The eyes of an indigo bunting are dark and are relatively large in size compared to its head, providing another identifying characteristic.
American robin: American robins are known for their characteristic orange or red breast and darker grey or black head and back.
The relative size of American robins is small compared to other objects in the image.
American robins typically have thin, yellow beaks, perfect for pulling earthworms out of the ground.
American robins have a distinct white ring around their eyes.
American robins have long legs that they use to hop around lawns and gardens while foraging for insects and berries.
In flight, American robins show a white underside with a deep orange-red breast, contrasting with the darker topside.
American robins are often seen on the ground with a characteristic upright posture.
bulbul: Bulbuls are medium-sized songbirds, often recognized by their distinctive crest or a rounded head on top.
Bulbuls typically have a sleek body with a long tail, which might be slim and pointed or fanned out depending on the species.
The relative size of a bulbul is smaller compared to other objects in the image.
Bulbuls usually have a short beak that is slightly curved downwards, suitable for their diet consisting of fruits, nectar, and insects.
Bulbul species cover a wide range of colors but most commonly, they are light brown or grey with some species having distinctive coloration around the eyes, throat or the underparts.
Many bulbul species have distinctive color patterns, like the red-whiskered bulbul with red face patch and whisker-marks, or the black-headed bulbul with a black head and greenish body.
Bulbuls are often located in forests or woodland areas, with some species adapting to urban environments.
jay: Jays are known for their vibrant blue and white or gray plumage, with each species having unique patterns and markings.
Jays are more prominent compared to their surroundings, often seen in trees, overground, or near bodies of water.
Most species of jays have a crest, a group of feathers on top of the bird's head that can be raised or lowered.
Jays have a substantial, solid body structure, with a round head, a sturdy bill, and solid wings.
Jays typically have broad, rounded wings and a long tail, which can vary in shape and size depending on the species.
The size of jays can vary, but they are normally larger than sparrows but smaller than crows.
Jays are known for their vocal behavior, often seen squawking or mimicking other birds' calls, making their presence noticeable in the image.
magpie: Magpies are easily identifiable by their characteristic black and white plumage.
Magpies have long tails, often nearly the same length as their bodies, which is a distinguishing feature.
The relative size of magpies is typically smaller compared to other objects in the image.
Magpies have strong, straight beaks that are somewhat elongated.
Their wings are broad with finger-like projections at the tips, visible when they are spread.
In flight, magpies exhibit a unique flight pattern of several quick flaps followed by a short glide, often with the wings held below the body.
On close view, one can identify the glossed feathers which can refract sunlight to give a bluish or purplish sheen.
chickadee: Chickadees are small birds known for their round body and large head in proportion to their body.
Chickadees are characterized by their black cap or crest and their black bib on the throat area, which contrasts with their white or grayish faces.
Chickadees have a short, thick, and slightly curved beak suitable for their diet of seeds, berries, and insects.
Chickadees have a short neck, which often makes their head seem directly attached to their bodies.
Chickadees are known for their agile flight pattern, often flitting from branch to branch.
Chickadees are commonly found in woodland environments and are often seen clinging upside down to the bottoms of branches.
Chickadees are known for their distinctive 'chick-a-dee' call from which they derive their name.
American dipper: American dippers are medium-sized birds, dark grey in color with a distinctive bobbing behavior.
American dippers have a short tail which constantly flicks up and down giving them a distinctive look.
They have a unique white eyelid that is visible when they blink.
They are noted for their ability to walk along riverbeds and streambeds under water to feed.
Their legs are strong and their toes have small, sharp claws, which are adaptations for their aquatic lifestyle.
They are usually solitary birds and are found near fast-flowing streams and rivers.
American dippers have a chunky appearance with a large head relative to their body size.
kite (bird of prey): Kite birds are medium-to-large birds of prey, distinctly known for their pointed wings and forked tail, attributing to their agile flying ability.
Their body color ranges from light brown to dark grey, often with white or lighter colored patches, particularly on the head and underparts.
Kites possess sharp and strong beak that is ideally suited for their carnivorous dietary habits.
Kites generally have a medium size, comparable to the size of a crow or slightly larger.
The eyes of a kite are sharp and striking, offering them keen vision for hunting prey.
Kites are usually noticed in open or semi-open habitats, soaring gracefully in the air at great heights.
Some species of kites, like the black kite, have unique marks or patterns on their plumage.
bald eagle: Bald eagles are large birds of prey known for their distinctive white head and tail, contrasting with a dark brown body and wings.
The bald eagle has a very large and powerful build, with a heavy body, large head and a hooked beak.
The beak of a bald eagle is large, hooked and yellow in color, designed for ripping flesh.
The bald eagle is often seen in posture of flat, horizontal wings and upright position, when perching, they sit upright.
The bald eagle's talons are strong and large, used for catching and carrying heavy prey.
Their eyes are also large and yellow, contributing to a very keen eyesight.
They also have a broad wingspan, ranging from 1.8 to 2.3 meters, which assists them in attaining high speed and precise maneuverability during flight.
vulture: Vultures are large birds that are commonly associated with their bald head and neck, which distinguish them from most other birds.
These birds are known for their powerful and wide wings, which they use to soar for long periods without tiring.
Vultures often appear in shades of brown to black, with some species having distinctive lighter or white patches or bands on the wings or tail.
Vultures have sharp, hooked beaks suited for tearing flesh.
The size of vultures is relatively large compared to other birds in the image.
Vultures are often seen high in the sky or perched in tall trees or on cliff faces, a behavior they exhibit when scanning for carrion to feed on.
Vultures have strong and sturdy legs with powerful talons.
great grey owl: The great grey owl is known for its large size, often described as the world's largest species of owl.
This owl is recognized for its big, rounded head with no ear tufts, and a grey face surrounded by a concentric ring pattern.
It has a long tail, the longest of all owl species, with a light barring pattern on it.
The body of the great grey owl is covered in a combination of light and dark feathers giving them a streaky, blotchy appearance.
Its upper parts are grey with pale bars; underparts are light with dark streaks.
The wings of the great grey owl are large and rounded.
Great grey owls have bright yellow eyes that stand out against the grey plumage.
fire salamander: Fire salamanders are known for their striking skin color, which is typically black with bright yellow to orange-red markings.
The body shape of fire salamanders is elongated, with a long tail and a wide, flattened head.
The relative size of fire salamanders is generally small to medium compared to other objects in the image. They can grow up to 20-25 cm in length.
Fire salamanders have two pairs of limbs that are relatively short and robust.
Fire salamanders have moist, smooth skin covered in mucus to keep their bodies humid and prevent desiccation.
The eyes of fire salamanders are quite distinctive: they are large, round, and protrude slightly from their heads.
Fire salamanders are typically found in humid environments, so you may see elements like water, wet leaves or moss in the image.
smooth newt: Smooth newts are small, growing up to 10 centimeters long, with females being slightly larger than males.
They are usually dark brown or grey in color, with an orange or yellow belly that is speckled with rounded black spots.
Smooth newts have a distinctive crest along the back and tail, which is more developed in males during the breeding season.
Compared to other objects in the image, the relative size of smooth newts is small.
They have a long, slender body with a tail that is flattened on the sides to aid in swimming.
Smooth newts have four limbs, each ending in sharp claws that help them in climbing and digging.
Their eyes are black and alert, giving them a watchful look.
newt: Newts are small amphibians, with most species reaching only about 4 inches in length.
They often have a brightly colored skin, which can be orange, red, yellow, or green in color.
Newt skin is typically smooth and appears wet because they secrete a slimy substance.
Newts have a long, slender body and a flattened head, which differentiates them from salamanders.
They have four short legs, all of which end in four or five toes.
Most species of newt have a distinctive paddle-like tail that aids in swimming.
Newts possess specific formations on their bodies according to their life stages, such as external gills during their aquatic larval stages.
spotted salamander: Spotted salamanders are known for their dark body color, usually black or dark bluish-black, dotted with bright yellow or orange spots.
Spotted salamanders have a stout body with a broad head and a blunt snout.
The relative size of spotted salamanders is smaller compared to other objects in the image.
Spotted salamanders have four short legs each ending in four toes in the front and five toes in the back.
Spotted salamanders have a long tail which is rounded at the base and tapers towards the end.
They usually have a smooth skin texture with a slimy coating, typical of many amphibians.
The position of its eyes on the head gives it a slightly 'upward looking' appearance.
axolotl: Axolotl are aquatic and are usually found underwater.
Axolotl have a wide and flat head with a mouth that spans the width of its head.
Axolotl have unique feathery gills, which are extremely distinctive and typically sit on either side of their head.
Axolotl have short legs with thin digits, and they have a tail fin for swimming.
The skin of axolotl is smooth and usually a variety of colors, including white (often referred to as leucistic), wild (dark with gold specks), and golden albino.
Axolotl are relatively small in size, usually ranging from 6 to 14 inches in length.
Axolotl have small, lidless eyes that make them look like they are always smiling.
American bullfrog: American bullfrogs are known for their green or greenish-brown coloration, often with darker spots or markings.
Bullfrogs are the largest frogs in North America, being on average 3.6 to 6 inches in body length, and their relative size compared to other objects in the image is noticeably larger.
They have a robust, stocky body and a broad, flat head.
They have noticeably large, circular eyes positioned at the top of their heads, allowing them to see above the water while most of their body remains submerged.
They have webbed hind feet which aids them in swimming, while their front feet have short, stubby toes.
They have distinctive eardrums or tympanum, which are circular and located behind the eyes. In males, these are larger than the eyes, whereas in females, they are about the same size as the eyes.
The mouth of a bullfrog is wide, and the upper lip is often green, while the lower lip is often yellow or white.
tree frog: Tree frogs are typically smaller than other types of frog, and their size can provide important distinguishing information in images.
Tree frogs often have slim bodies with long, thin limbs, designed for climbing and jumping in their arboreal habitats.
Tree frogs have distinctive, large, round eyes that are crucial for spotting predators and prey at night. The eyes may have vertical iris slits or unique patterns in different species.
Some species of tree frog are brightly colored, such as the red-eyed tree frog with its vibrant green body and red eyes, while others have a more muted coloration for camouflage.
The feet of tree frogs are equipped with round, adhesive toe pads, which assist them in climbing and provide a unique visual attribute.
Tree frogs can often be seen gripping onto vertical surfaces or hanging from branches or leaves, thanks to their unique climbing abilities.
Some species of tree frog have visible tympanums (ear drums) behind the eyes, which can be used as an identifying attribute.
tailed frog: Tailed frogs are known for their distinctive tail-like structure, called the 'coccyx,' which is actually an extension of the male frog's reproductive organ.
Tailed frogs are relatively small, typically measuring between 1 to 2 inches in length, which includes the tail.
Tailed frogs have a robust body with a broad, flat head and short limbs.
These frogs have a unique trait of having vertical pupils in their eyes, which differentiate them from their closely related species.
Tailed frogs have well-developed discs on their fingers, which helps them cling to rocks in fast-moving streams.
Their skin color varies from brown to green or grey, often with darker spots or blotches, and their bellies are typically white or cream-colored.
The female tailed frog can be distinguished from the male by her larger size and lack of 'tail'.
loggerhead sea turtle: Loggerhead sea turtles have a large, heavy, and muscular head.
These sea turtles have a larger shell compared to their body size.
The color of the loggerhead's shell generally ranges from reddish-brown to brown or sometimes black.
The underside of the loggerhead, the plastron, is usually yellow or light brown
Loggerhead sea turtles can be found in the ocean, so often seen in a marine environment in the images.
Loggerhead sea turtles typically have thick, slightly curved, and strong front flippers to help them swim effectively.
These sea turtles have a hooked beak shape jaw which gives them the name 'loggerhead'.
leatherback sea turtle: Recognizable by its large size, the leatherback sea turtle is the largest turtle species and one of the largest living reptiles.
Unlike most sea turtles, the leatherback's carapace is covered by skin and oily flesh instead of a hard bony shell.
They have distinct long, paddle-like flippers, making them adept swimmers.
Known for its teardrop-shaped body, which is more streamlined for swimming compared to other turtles.
The color of a leatherback can vary but is typically dark grey or black with white or pink spots.
Leatherbacks have a unique pattern of ridges on their carapace, typically with seven longitudinal ridges.
Leatherbacks often venture into colder waters, thanks to unique adaptations like countercurrent heat exchangers and a large body mass.
mud turtle: Mud turtles are small, typically ranging from 3 to 4 inches in length.
They have a dark, domed upper shell (carapace) that is usually brown or black in color.
The lower shell (plastron) is usually yellowish with dark blotches.
They have a very short, pointy tail.
Mud turtles have a distinctive head with large eyes and a sharply pointed snout.
They have strong, clawed feet which they use for digging in mud.
Mud turtles live in slow-moving or still bodies of water and are often found near or in the mud.
terrapin: Terrapins are often associated with their unique shell. It is typically a dull brown color and covered in scutes or plates.

They are known for having a hard shell that covers their back (carapace) and a lighter one on their underside (plastron). Most terrapins can retract their head and limbs into their shell for protection.
Terrapins have a strong and sharp beak which is characteristic of all turtles. It allows them to cut and chew their food.
Terrapins have a small tail, which is often more noticeable in male terrapins.
Terrapins have short and sturdy legs. Those in front have sharp claws, helping them in digging and climbing.
Terrapins are semi-aquatic, so they are often captured in or near bodies of water, such as swamps, ponds, or marshes.
Depending on the species, terrapins can vary in size, though many commonly found terrapins are somewhere around 5 to 12 inches in length.
box turtle: Box turtles have high, dome-like shells that can vary in color, with patterns of yellow, orange, or brown on a black or dark green background.
The shells of box turtles are hinged at the bottom, allowing the turtles to completely close their shells for protection.
Box turtles have stocky, strong legs with sharp claws, which are adapted for digging and traversing different terrains.
The plastron, or lower shell, of a box turtle is usually light-colored and relatively unmarked.
Box turtles have strong, curved beaks and no teeth.
The skin of a box turtle can be colorful like its shell, often marked with yellow or orange spots on a dark background.
Box turtles have large, expressive eyes, typically with a dark iris surrounded by a ring of color that can vary from red to yellow.
banded gecko: Banded geckos are known for their distinctive colouration, featuring alternating bands of light and dark colours across their bodies.
They are relatively small lizards, with a length from snout to tail base typically ranging from 3 to 6 inches.
They possess a slightly flattened body, a large head relative to the body, and have vertical pupil in their eyes.
Their tails are rounded and bulky, often with stark color banding. The tail can be shed and regrown as a survival tactic.
They have pad-like structures on the undersides of their fingers and toes, allowing them to cling and climb on a variety of surfaces.
Banded geckos often inhabit desert or rocky habitats, and may be seen hiding in the crevices during the day.
They are nocturnal animals and their activities primarily occur during the night.
green iguana: Green iguanas are well known for their vibrant green color, which can vary from bright lime green to a more subdued olive or teal.
Green iguanas are large lizards, with adults typically reaching lengths of 5 to 7 feet including their tail, which accounts for about half of their total length.
Green iguanas have a row of spines running down their back from the neck to the tip of their tail. The spines on their back are larger and more pronounced than those on their belly and sides.
Green iguanas have a distinctive 'dewlap', a flap of skin that hangs down under their chin, which can be inflated when the iguana is feeling threatened or wants to display dominance.
Green iguanas have a 'third eye' on top of their head, technically known as the parietal eye, which is sensitive to changes in light and can detect movement from above.
Green iguanas have strong, muscular limbs with sharp claws that they use for climbing and defending themselves.
Green iguanas have a long tail which they can whip at high speed as a form of defense. They also have the ability to detach their tail if caught by a predator.
Carolina anole: Carolina anoles are small lizards typically ranging from 5 to 8 inches in length including their tail.
Carolina anoles have a slim, elongated body shape, with a long, thin tail.
They are known for their ability to change color, usually being green or brown, depending on their mood, temperature, humidity, or health.
Male Carolina anoles have a large, fan-like flap of skin, known as a dewlap, beneath their necks, which can be extended for displays of aggression or courtship.
Carolina anoles have smooth scaled skin, which may have a slightly dewy or shiny appearance.
The eyes of Carolina anoles are relatively large compared to their head size, with a distinct round pupil and a golden irises.
Carolina anoles have relatively long, slim legs suitable for climbing and jumping from branches, and they are often observed in trees or shrubs.
desert grassland whiptail lizard: This species can be recognized for its elongated and slender body.
It has a distinctive leopard-like pattern with dark spots on a greenish or yellowish skin, allowing it to blend into its desert surroundings.
The tail of this lizard species is usually longer than its body, used as a counterbalance during fast movement.
They have long, thin legs perfect for running at a fast pace.
The size of this lizard is relatively small as compared to other objects in the image.
These lizards are exclusively female and reproduce through parthenogenesis, i.e. they lay unfertilized eggs that develop into clones of the mother.
This species of lizard is typically found with a rugged, desert-style background in their photos.
agama: Agamas can have a variety of colors, with males often more brightly colored than females. The dominant males tend to be bright blue or red.
Agamas have a broad, flat head, long tail and relatively short legs, which can help in identification.
Agamas are mainly found in the wild in arid, rocky environments. They often bask on rocks in the sun.
Agamas are medium-sized reptiles, measuring between 7.5 to 15 inches long, including the tail.
Agamas are often seen in a defensive posture, standing high on their legs with their body off the ground and tail raised.
They have the capability to change their color in response to changes in temperature, mood or their surroundings.
In a resting or cold state, the dominant male's color will be dark brown and less vibrant.
frilled-necked lizard: These lizards are famous for their large ruff, or 'frill' around their neck which flares out when threatened or mating.
Their color can range from reddish-brown to grey to nearly black, often mimicking the soil or rock color of their habitats.
The frill, when extended, can show bright colors such as red, orange, or yellow, depending on the lizard's mood or intention.
These lizards are relatively large, commonly reaching up to 85-95 centimeters in total length, making them one of the larger species of lizards.
They have a long, slender body with a large head and mouth which allows them to consume a variety of prey.
The legs of frilled-necked lizards are long and powerful, enabling them to run quickly and even on their hind legs.
These lizards have a forked tongue, similar to that of a snake, which they use for smelling.
alligator lizard: Alligator lizards have elongated, narrow bodies and are typically green, brown, or grey in color with yellow or white bellies.
They have distinctive scales that are rough and keeled, giving them an armored look similar to alligators.
Alligator lizards have long tails that can make up over half of their total length, and these tails can break off as a defense mechanism.
They have small, sharp teeth which they use to catch prey like insects, spiders, and small mammals.
Alligator lizards have powerful limbs and sharp claws for climbing and catching prey.
Their eyes are surrounded by scaled eyelids and have vertical pupils.
They have a forked tongue that they use for smelling and tasting their environment, similar to snakes.
Gila monster: Gila monsters are known for their distinctive, vibrant skin patterns which include a blotted pattern of bright pink, orange, or yellow mixed with black.
They are one of the few venomous lizards in the world, with venom glands located in their lower jaw.
Gila monsters have a broad, flat head with rounded snout, small eyes, and stout body ending with a short tail which is used to store fat.
They possess strong limbs with sharp claws that are designed for digging and climbing.
Its size relative to other objects in the image is medium, as adult Gila monsters usually grow to about a foot and a half in length.
Unlike other lizards, Gila monsters possess a beaded skin texture.
Gila monsters are typically found in desert or semi-arid regions, often in rocky or sandy habitats.
European green lizard: As the name implies, these lizards are typically bright green, but can also exhibit shades from dull olive to luminous emerald.
They are known for the vibrant blue spots or stripes on their sides, which can be especially prominent in males during the mating season.
The body shape is elongated with a long slender tail, which can be up to twice the length of the body.
They are medium-sized lizards, with males reaching lengths up to 16 inches, including the tail.
They have small, round, overlapping scales, giving their skin a slightly granular appearance.
The lizards have well-developed limbs with five digits on each foot equipped with sharp claws for climbing and gripping.
They have a distinct head with clearly visible nostrils and eyes, the latter often exhibiting a brightly colored iris.
chameleon: Chameleons are known for their striking color-changing ability, varying from green, blue, turquoise to even more exotic colors like pink and purple under certain conditions.
Chameleons have highly distinctive body shapes with a raised back, conical head, and a prehensile tail that can tightly curl.
The size of a chameleon can help in its identification. They can vary in size from small species that only reach a few inches in length, to much larger species that can be over a foot long.
Chameleons have unique eyes that can move independently from each other, providing a full 360-degree arc of vision.
They are characterized by their zygodactylous feet - on each foot, the five toes are fused into a group of two and a group of three, giving them a tongs-like appearance.
Many species have a prehensile tail which they use for balance and grip when moving through trees and shrubs.
Some species of chameleons have a small horn on their forehead or rostral protuberance.
Komodo dragon: Komodo dragons are the largest living lizards in the world, and their overall size compared to other objects in the image is large.
They are heavy-bodied animals, with a flat head, bowed legs, and long, thick tail.
They have a distinct brown or grayish color, with dry, rough, and scaly skin.
They have sharp teeth and a long, yellow, deeply forked tongue.
They are predominantly terrestrial and are often seen on ground level in images.
They inhabit hot, tropical areas and are native to the Indonesian islands, so images may contain these elements.
A distinctive attribute is the young Komodo dragons, which have a distinct pattern of green, yellow, and black bands, which fades as they mature.
Nile crocodile: Nile crocodiles have a dark bronze colouration with black cross-banding across the body and tail.
They have a long, broad body with a large head and long heavy jaws, which is an identifying feature.
The relative size of a Nile crocodile is typically larger compared to other objects in the image as they are known to reach a maximum length of about 6 meters.
They have a row of shielding along the back and the tail, which is distinctive of crocodiles.
The Nile crocodile's eyes and nostrils are located on the top of its head allowing it to see and breathe while the rest of its body is underwater.
They have a strong tail for powerful swimming and rear limbs with webbing between the toes to aid movement in water.
Nile crocodiles are notorious for their aggressive nature and are often seen lurking just below the surface of the water.
American alligator: American alligators are large reptiles, typically dark grey or black in color.
They have a powerful, flat tail that they use for propulsion in the water and for defense on land.
They have a thick, armored body with a muscular, flat tail.
They have a large mouth filled with sharp, conical teeth for catching and holding prey.
The eyes and nostrils of American alligators are on top of their heads, allowing them to breathe and see when the rest of their body is underwater.
Fully grown males are 10 to 15 feet in length, making them larger than most other objects in the image.
They are primarily aquatic, often found in freshwater environments like rivers, lakes, swamps, and marshes.
triceratops: Triceratops is a type of dinosaur known for their three distinctive horns - two long ones above the eyes and a smaller one on the nose.
Triceratops have a large, circular shield-like frill on their head that extends from the eyes to the neck for protection.
Triceratops is a quadrupedal dinosaur, meaning they walked on all four legs, with robust limbs that ended in hoof-like claws.
They are known to have a large, heavy body that can be comparable to that of an elephant.
Triceratops have a bird-like beaked mouth, which they used for biting and cutting plant material.
Despite being herbivorous, Triceratops are often depicted in a confrontational stance with predator dinosaurs, mainly the T-rex, highlighting their role as defensive herbivores.
Triceratops are generally depicted with a gray or brown color, but there is no scientific consensus on their true skin color or pattern.
worm snake: The worm snake, as suggested by its name, is often mistaken for a worm due to its slim, elongated body which is generally brown or pinkish in color.
They are typically small, usually less than a foot long.
Their body is cylindrical and slightly tapered at both ends, mimicking the earthworm's form.
Unlike the scales of most other snakes, the one on worm snakes are smooth and glossy, giving them a slightly shiny appearance.
Their tiny eyes are covered by scales, making them look almost eyeless.
Worm snakes have a pointed tail tip, which they use to probe their surroundings.
Being a fossorial species, they are often found burrowing in leaf litter or loose soil.
ring-necked snake: Most ring-necked snakes are small and slender, typically reaching lengths of 10 to 15 inches.
Ring-necked snakes have a distinctly colored ring around their neck, often in bright yellow or orange, contrasting with their dark bodies.
The dorsal color of ring-necked snakes can vary from blue-gray to black, while their undersides are brightly colored, often yellow or red, sometimes with an irregular black pattern.
Ring-necked snakes have round pupils and may exhibit an 'S' shaped defensive posture when threatened.
Ring-necked snakes predominantly inhabit forested environments and are often found under logs, rocks, or leaf litter.
As nocturnal animals, they are most often encountered at night.
They are non-venomous creatures, predominantly feeding on smaller reptiles, amphibians, and insects.
eastern hog-nosed snake: They are known for their upturned snout, which gives them their 'hog-nosed' name.
They are known to have thick bodies with keeled scales and their color can vary between brown, gray, olive, orange, and more.
The snake's body is relatively short compared to other species, with an average length of 20 to 33 inches.
They have a distinctive defensive behavior, they flatten their neck and raise their head off the ground, similar to a cobra.
Their unique attribute is that they are known to play dead when threatened, rolling onto their back and opening their mouth.
They have round pupils, unlike other venomous snakes in North America that typically have elliptical pupils.
Their belly is usually lighter in color, commonly yellow or grey, with darker markings.
smooth green snake: This reptile is known for its distinctive bright green coloration which helps it blend in with foliage.
Smooth green snakes are small and slender, generally measuring around 12 to 20 inches in length.
These snakes have smooth scales, giving them a glossy appearance and justifying their name.
Smooth green snakes have a very pointed snout, which differentiates them from many other snake species.
They have round pupils and their eyes are relatively large in comparison to their head size.
These snakes typically have a yellow or pale underside contrasting with their vibrant green topside.
Smooth green snakes are non-venomous and have very small, rear-facing teeth.
kingsnake: Kingsnakes come in a variety of colors and patterns, most commonly having bands or stripes that are black, red, yellow, or white.
The body of a kingsnake is cylindrical and muscular, allowing it to constrict and subdue its prey.
Relative to other objects in the image, kingsnakes can range from small to quite large, growing up to 7 feet in length.
Kingsnakes have a pair of eyes on the sides of their head, which are covered by clear scales instead of eyelids.
Kingsnakes have a single, unbroken dorsal stripe running along the length of their body in some variants.
The head of a kingsnake is somewhat distinct from its neck, an identification mark for most snake species.
Kingsnakes have smooth glossy scales, giving their body a shiny appearance.
garter snake: Garter snakes are small to medium-sized snakes, typically ranging from 20 to 30 inches in length.
They have long, slender bodies and are known for their distinctive longitudinal stripes, which can vary in color but are often yellow, white or red against a darker body color.
Garter snakes have a head that is wider than the neck, giving it a distinct shape.
They have round pupils and relatively large eyes compared to the size of their head, which distinguishes them from venomous snakes in North America that typically have vertical, slit-like pupils.
Garter snakes have smooth scales and their skin often has a glossy sheen.
They are mostly terrestrial snakes and are often found in habitats near water - they are good swimmers as well.
Garter snakes are nonvenomous, known for their docile nature, and in case of danger, they prefer to escape rather than attack.
water snake: Water snakes are generally found in water bodies and are known for their good swimming abilities.
They are longer and thinner as compared to many snakes and have a distinct rusty, brownish or greenish, sometimes dark color.
Water snakes usually have a variety of patterns on their body which can include stripes and blotchy patterns.
Their belly is often paler and can have a checkered pattern.
They typically have a round pupil and their heads are broad and flat.
Water snakes have a long, undulating body and are typically captured in motion in water or very close to it.
They lack rattles at the ends of their tails, a feature of venomous snakes, making them common subjects of confusion.
vine snake: Vine snakes are slender reptiles known for their resemblance to green vines, both in color and shape.
They have long, slim bodies that can stretch out to all lengths, emulating the shape of actual vines.
Vine snakes are primarily green, which helps them blend into their forest environment. But they can also exhibit other colors.
Unique to vine snakes are their pointed muzzles, which help them catch prey.
Vine snakes have large, bulging eyes which allow for exceptional vision. Their eyes are usually yellow or gold in color.
The body length of vine snakes can reach up to 1.5 meters, which is quite long compared to other objects in the image.
They are known for their slightly keeled scales, which are scaly protrusions on their skin that make them look more like a vine.
night snake: Night snakes are generally pale gray or cream in color, with distinctive large, dark brown or black blotches and spots across their back and sides.
They are generally small to medium-sized snakes, with adults typically reaching lengths of up to 30 inches.
A unique characteristic of night snakes is their vertical, elliptical pupils, similar to those of a cat, which helps them see better at night.
Another feature that distinguishes night snakes is the presence of a dark, inverted V or H shape on their neck or head.
They have a pointed head and a slender body, typical of many nocturnal snake species.
Their tail is short and tapering, ending in a pointed tip.
Night snakes are known for their secretive and mostly nocturnal behavior, often hiding under rocks or in burrows during the day.
boa constrictor: Boa constrictors are characterized by a square and muscular body, capable of exerting a significant amount of pressure to restrict their prey.
A distinguishing characteristic of the boa constrictor is their skin pattern that consists of saddle or bowtie-like brown or reddish-brown patterns down its back.
The skin between the patterns is cream or tan and emits a mother of pearl shimmer in sunlight due to embedded crystalline structures.
They also have triangular head shapes that are larger than their neck, with a clear distinction between the two.
Another feature is the presence of pits between their nostrils and eyes which detect the heat of their prey.
Boa constrictors have elliptical pupils, unlike many other snakes which have round pupils.
The scales under a boa's tail (cloacal scales) have a distinct pattern and size, differentiating male boa constrictors from females.
African rock python: African rock pythons have a muscular, tubular body that is covered in rough, reticulated scales. They are one of the largest species of snake in the world.
The coloration of these snakes typically ranges from olive green to brown with irregularly shaped patches or bands that are darker in color.
African rock pythons have a distinctive head that is covered in small scales, with a clear separation from the neck. Their eyes have vertical, elliptical pupils.
The python's large size in comparison to other snakes or objects in the image can be a key identifying feature.
African rock pythons have large scales on their bellies, which are used for gripping surfaces as they move.
African rock pythons are ambush predators, and are often seen coiled up in a hiding spot before striking.
These pythons are non-venomous and kill their prey by constriction. They are capable of eating large prey items due to their ability to dislocate their jaws.
Indian cobra: This snake is known by its prominent hood, which is flared out when the snake feels threatened or agitated.
Indian cobras have a characteristic mark on the underside of their hood, which looks similar to a pair of spectacles or eyes.
The color of the Indian cobra can vary but commonly they are a light to medium brown color.
This species is medium-sized, ranging from 3.3 to 5.9 feet in length, which can be determined relative to other objects in the image.
Their body shape is slender, and their head is not significantly wider than their body.
The scales of the Indian Cobra are smooth, and their belly scales are broad and oblong.
Indian Cobras are usually found in open forests, fields, and also close to human settlement because they prey on rodents.
green mamba: This snake is typically bright green, and may also occasionally have yellow or blue hues, setting it apart from others in its environment.
Green mambas typically have slim, elongated bodies. Their length can reach up to about 2 meters.
This snake exhibits a head that is slightly distinct from the neck and has a coffin-shaped appearance when viewed from above.
The eyes of a green mamba are medium-sized with round pupils and are generally a striking green or gold color.
Green mambas live mainly in the trees and are rarely found on the ground, so pictures may often include surrounding foliage or be in a tree
Despite their vivid color, green mamba's are known for their excellent camouflage among foliage, often hiding among leaves, so part of it may be hidden or blend with the environment.
The scales on a green mamba are smooth and have a glossy appearance.
sea snake: Sea snakes are known for their long, slender bodies which can be of various colors including black, blue-grey, and even yellow or green.
Typically, sea snakes have small flattened heads which distinguish them from land snakes.
Their bodies are often covered in patterns or bands, though the design can vary depending on the particular species.
Sea snakes possess paddle-like tails, adapted for swimming.
Some species of sea snakes have fangs located at the rear of their mouths, a feature unique from other types of snakes.
They are fully adapted to life in water, so they are often seen in marine environments such as oceans, coastal lines, or coral reefs.
The size of sea snakes can vary considerably depending on the species, they can range from 120 cm to 3 m in length.
Saharan horned viper: This snake species is known for its pale sandy color, which helps it camouflage in its desert habitat.
One of the most distinctive traits of this snake are the 'horns' or projections above each eye.
The snake has a scale-patterning that typically consists of a series of dark, dorsolateral triangles.
Its body is relatively thick and its head is distinguishable by a wide neck, which is characteristic of vipers.
They can grow to lengths between 30-85 cm, so in images, they might appear smaller or larger depending on their current growth.
It has a distinctive arrow-shaped head and vertically elliptical, yellow to golden yellow eyes.
The snake's tail ends in a horny spur, which is mildly venomous.
eastern diamondback rattlesnake: They are recognized for their diamond-shaped patterns, which are dark brown or black with a lighter brown or yellow outline.
This type of snake can be quite large, with the average adult reaching lengths of 4 to 6 feet.
They are known for their distinct rattling sound, made by a segmented rattle at the tip of their tail when the snake vibrates its tail.
These snakes have a triangular-shaped head that is distinct and separate from the body.
The snake's body is thick and strong, it is the heaviest venomous snake in America and the largest rattlesnake species.
The color of these snakes is typically brown or grey with an intricate diamond pattern along their body.
It can be found in sandy and dry habitats, longleaf pine savannas, and coastal scrub habitats. So, any image might often include such backgrounds.
sidewinder rattlesnake: Sidewinder rattlesnakes have a distinctive 'sidewinding' movement which involves throwing their body in a looped motion.
They are known for their color that well-camouflaged with the desert sand, typically a pale sandy color with dark dorsal blotches.
The overall body shape of a sidewinder rattlesnake is slim and long, with a distinct 'diamond' or 'triangular' shaped head.
The scales on their body are keeled, which give them a rough appearance.
They have a unique adaptation of two raised patches over their eyes that functions as protection from sand and also serve to intimidate potential threats.
The relative size of a sidewinder rattlesnake is small, generally ranging from 20 inches to 30 inches in length.
They typically have a rattle at the end of their tail which they use as a warning signal to potential threats.
trilobite: Trilobites are fossilized marine arthropods with a distinctive three-lobed, three-segmented form.
Trilobites range in size from tiny to over two feet long, but most species were under three inches long.
Though extinct, they are considered highly recognizable due to their distinct appearance in fossil form.
They had a semi-circular or oval-shaped head shield called cephalon, a segmented body or thorax, and a tail piece or pygidium.
The body is divided into three vertical lobes, with the central lobe known as the axis and the lateral lobes on either side known as pleurae.
Depending on the species their exoskeleton could have been smooth, pitted, or covered in spines.
Some had complex eyes, while others had no eyes at all.
harvestman: Harvestmen are characterized by elongated bodies, unlike the typical compact shape of many spiders and insects.
One key feature of harvestmen are their incredibly long and thin legs, which can be several times the length of their bodies.
Unlike spiders, harvestmen have a fused body, meaning their abdomen and cephalothorax are joined together without a visible constriction in the middle.
Harvestmen have two eyes located in the middle of their bodies. The eyes are usually black and prominent.
Harvestmen move in a distinctive bouncing or wobbling manner due to their long, slender legs.
They are typically brown or grayish in color, allowing them to blend in with wood and foliage.
In relation to other objects in the photo, harvestmen are small, with bodies rarely exceeding one inch in length, though their legs stretch out much further.
scorpion: Scorpions are known for their unique body structure, composed of a cephalothorax (head) and a segmented tail, often curving upwards and tipped with a venomous stinger.
Scorpions have two large grasping pincers called pedipalps which they use to catch prey.
The body length of most scorpions ranges between 2.5 to 22 cm, which can give a hint about the relative size of a scorpion in an image.
Most scorpions are nocturnal creatures, which may affect the lighting and environment in the image.
Scorpions are generally found in desert or arid environments. This can be a helpful context clue in identifying them in images.
Scorpions are often a yellowish-brown or tan color, although some species can be darker or brighter in color.
Scorpions have eight legs like other arachnids.
yellow garden spider: Yellow garden spiders have distinct coloration, primarily black and yellow.
They are identified by their relatively large size, with females being significantly larger than males.
These spiders have an oval abdomen and a smaller cephalothorax connected by a narrow waist.
They often build large, orb-shaped webs in gardens, fields, and on the side of buildings
The web might have a unique zig-zag pattern at its center, known as the stabilimentum.
They are often found in a head-down position in the web's center during daytime
Yellow garden spiders are found during warm months; they aren't typically sighted during winter.
barn spider: Barn spiders have a rounded abdomen and are often a dark brown color with lighter markings.
They have a classic 'spider' appearance with a bulbous abdomen and long legs.
The barn spider's legs are typically dark brown or black with lighter bands.
Barn spiders have a large web spun in a circular form.
Barn spiders are sizable and can range in size from 10mm to 20mm in body length, not including their legs.
Barn spiders are often found hanging upside down in their web.
A common orb-weaver spider found in barns and other structures. It spins large, circular webs to catch insects and is known for its distinctive yellow and brown markings.
European garden spider: They are known for their distinctive cross or 'X' shaped pattern on their abdomen in lighter colors, against a brown or black background.
European garden spiders are often found in gardens, they create large often intricate orb-webs to catch their prey.
The relative size of the European garden spider is small compared to other objects in the image.
They have eight legs which are divided into two rows on the cephalothorax.
European garden spiders have a large round abdomen and a smaller cephalothorax to which their legs are attached.
The size varies, with females being larger, up to 15 mm, and males being smaller, up to 5 mm.
They sometimes play dead as a defense mechanism when disturbed.
southern black widow: This spider is known for its shiny, black body. Females have a red hourglass-shaped marking on the underside of their abdomen.
A distinctive attribute of the southern black widow is the presence of red spots or bars on the dorsal side of the abdomen, unlike the northern black widow that only has hourglass markings.
Their legs are long and slender and are also black in color.
They are typically found in dark, sheltered environments like woodpiles, under stones, or in hollow tree stumps.
They are known to create messy and irregular cobwebs, which can be another identifying attribute.
Southern black widows have eight eyes arranged in two rows, a common feature in most spiders.
They are solitary creatures and are normally not found in groups.
tarantula: Tarantulas are known for their heavy, robust bodies and their hairy appearance.
Tarantulas have eight legs, and their body is divided into two segments: the cephalothorax and the abdomen.
The size of a tarantula can vary significantly with species, but many are relatively large compared to other spiders.
Some tarantulas exhibit distinctive color patterns, such as the Mexican red-knee tarantula which has bright red bands on its legs.
Their large, pointed fangs are characteristic, although they're not usually visible unless the tarantula is feeding or feeling threatened.
Tarantulas possess appendages close to their mouth known as pedipalps, which could be mistaken for an extra pair of legs.
Tarantulas are terrestrial and tend to be reclusive, often seen hiding or in burrows.
wolf spider: Wolf spiders are noticeable by their eyes arrangement - they have eight eyes arranged in three rows: four small eyes in the lowest row, two larger eyes in the middle and two medium-sized eyes in the top row.
Wolf spiders range in size but are generally bulky and robust, with body lengths ranging from 10 to 35mm.
Unlike many other spiders, wolf spiders don't build webs. Instead, they are hunters and may be seen roaming across the ground or waiting to ambush their prey.
They have eight legs, with the front pair typically longer and stronger that are adapted for the hunting lifestyle.

Wolf spiders carry their egg sac at the end of their bodies attached to their spinnerets. Once the spiderlings hatch, they climb onto their mother's back and stay there until they are fully developed.
They have two prominent, large jaws (chelicerae) which they use for hunting and feeding.
Wolf spiders live in a wide range of habitats, including forests, grasslands, wet coastal forests, gardens and homes.
tick: Ticks are small, spider-like creatures that range in size from a pin-head to a pencil eraser. They can expand significantly when engorged with blood.
They have eight legs situating them in the arachnid family along with spiders and mites.
Ticks come in a variety of colors, most commonly shades of brown or reddish-brown, but can also be cream-colored or grayish-white, especially when engorged.
Ticks do not have wings and move around by crawling or attaching to hosts.

The body of a tick is divided into two sections: the smaller anterior capitulum (or gnathosoma), which contains the mouthparts, and the larger posterior idiosoma, which contains the legs, digestive tract, and reproductive organs.
Ticks are most often found in tall grass, thick brush, or wooded areas where they can easily attach to passing hosts.
The body of ticks swells and can turn a grayish color after a blood meal, which is necessary for them to progress to each stage of their life cycle.
centipede: Centipedes are known for their long, segmented bodies with each segment having a pair of legs.
Centipedes are typically brown or reddish-orange, but their color can vary depending on the species.
Centipedes have numerous legs, often with 15 to 177 pairs.
Centipedes have a pair of venomous claws known as forcipules which are located just behind the head.
Centipedes are elongated and can vary in size from few millimeters to 30 centimeters in length depending on the species.
The body of a centipede is flattened with segments being either smooth or with small bumps.
Centipedes have antennae made up of many segments, which are often longer in species that live in dark places.
black grouse: Black grouses are known for their distinctive black plumage, which is prominently displayed during mating displays.
Male black grouses, known as Blackcocks, have a striking red wattle over the eye, which is a distinctive feature against their black feathers.
Black grouses have lyre-shaped tails that are characteristic to them. Males display these in a unique mating ritual known as lekking.
The physical size of black grouses is larger compared to other birds. They can reach a body length of up to 55 cm (22 in).
The female black grouse, or greyhen, has a more muted color palette with mottled brown feathers, allowing them to blend in with their surroundings.
Black grouses have sturdy legs and are hardy birds, which is visible in their posture and physique.
Their habitat often includes snowy or cold environments, which can be a hint towards their identification when captured in their natural surroundings.
ptarmigan: Ptarmigans are often recognized by their compact, chicken-like build with short legs and wings.
Ptarmigans are known for their seasonal plumage, where they molt and change colours according to the seasons, white in winter and brown or grey in summer.
Ptarmigans have short, rounded tails that are often dark on the end.
The beak of a ptarmigan is short, stout and strong, adapted for a diet mainly consisting of buds, leaves, and twigs.
Male ptarmigans commonly have a red 'comb' above their eyes during the breeding season.
Ptarmigans are found in cold arctic and subarctic environments, often seen among snowy, icy or rocky landscapes.
Ptarmigans are usually seen on the ground, as they are not frequent fliers but they can fly when necessary.
ruffed grouse: Ruffed grouse are known for their medium size, with males weighing between 1 and 1.5 pounds and females weighing slightly less.
The ruffed grouse gets its name from the large ruff around its neck, which is especially noticeable in males during the mating season when they fan their feathers to display.
Ruffed grouse have a reddish-brown body with a darker back. Their plumage is finely patterned with grey, brown, and white.
These birds have a fan-shaped tail with a broad black band near the end. The tail carries a distinct pattern which helps in identification.
Ruffed grouse have small heads relative to their bodies and short, strong beaks.
Their eye color is usually yellowish-brown.
Ruffed grouse are not strong fliers and often prefer to walk or run on the ground, usually seen in habitats like forests and woodlands.
prairie grouse: Prairie grouses are typically characterized by their rounded body shape and robust shape.
They have a stout beak that is perfect for a diet of seeds and insects.
Prairie grouses have relatively short legs with sturdy claws for scratching the soil in search of food.
Most prairie grouses have a distinctive collar or band of contrasting color around their neck or breast.
The males typically have elaborate courtship displays which can include inflating air sacs on their neck, fanning out their tail feathers, and making unique sounds.
Prairie grouses are mostly terrestrial birds, meaning that they live on the ground, but they are capable of flying short distances when needed.
They are most often found in open prairie or grassland habitats where they forage for food and seek cover from predators.
peafowl: Peafowls are large and colorful birds with elongated upper-tail covert feathers which are marked with eye-spots.
The feathers of a male peafowl, or peacock, are often iridescent blue and green, with an elaborate eye-spotted 'tail' or 'train'.
Female peafowls, or peahens, are usually more muted in color, with a mixture of dull green, brown, and grey feathers.
The males are famous for their courtship display, where they fan out their long train and quiver these feathers to attract females.
Peafowls show sexual dimorphism, where males and females have different physical characteristics apart from their sex organs. Males are generally larger and more colorful.
Young peafowls, known as peachicks, are generally a greyish or brownish color for the first year of their life.
In terms of size, peafowls often grow to more than 1.5 metres in length, not including the tail feathers which can add an additional 1.5 metres.
quail: Quails are small, short-tailed birds with a rounded body and a distinctive crest on the head, which can be raised or lowered.
Quail plumage is often brownish with intricate patterns, helping them blend into their natural environment.
Relative to its body size, a quail's beak is short, curved, and strong, suitable for its predominantly granivorous diet.
Quails usually have short wings, which are adapted for explosive bursts of flight, an escape mechanism known as 'flushing'.
The quail's legs and feet are robust, enabling it to walk and run to escape predators rather than taking flight.
Male quails of many species have distinctive calls, with the male North American Bobwhite's call being recognized as 'bob-white', from which it gets its name.
Quails can be found in a variety of habitats depending on the species, from forests to deserts and grasslands.
partridge: Partridges generally have a plump body and a rounded shape, indicative of its ground-dwelling nature.
The color palette of a partridge typically blends with its natural habitat and can range from brown and grey to chestnut hues, often with intricate patterning.
Partridges typically have short, stout legs that are perfect for life on the ground and their toes are often feathered in certain species.
Partridges come equipped with a short, hard beak designed for pecking seeds and other food from the ground.
The size of the partridge is smaller compared to other objects in the image. Most species range from 24-35 cm in length.
Their wings are generally broad and rounded, indicative of short, rapid flight when disturbed.
Males and females can often be differentiated by their colouring or size, with males often larger and more brightly colored.
african grey parrot: They are predominantly grey, with accents of white and a red or maroon tail.
African greys have a robust, slender body shape and a broad wingspan.
The size of the african grey parrot is medium compared to other objects in the image.
They have strong, black beaks and grey feet.
African grey parrots have a distinct feather pattern that features scalloped feathers across the neck and backs.
African greys have a distinctive patch of white feathers around their eyes and beak.
African grey parrots have rounded, short tails.
macaw: Macaws are known for their vibrant, multi-colored plumage which can include green, blue, red, yellow, and other colors.
Macaws have a long, strong tail that helps them balance and steer when flying.
Macaws have a bare facial patch, which can be white, pink, or partly covered with short lines of feathers.
They have pointed wings, allowing them to fly faster in the wild.
Macaws are large birds; depending on the species, they can range from 12 inches to over 40 inches in length.
Macaws often pair for life and can often be seen in pairs, even while in a flock.
Macaws are often pictured perched on tree branches, as they are arboreal creatures and spend a lot of their time in trees in the wild.
sulphur-crested cockatoo: The sulphur-crested cockatoo has a predominantly white plumage which contrasts with its vibrant yellow crest.
The crest is the sulphur-crested cockatoo's most distinctive feature, large and curved, which can be raised or lowered depending on the bird's emotional state.
Their beak is large, powerful, and grey-black, used for cracking open hard nuts and seeds.
They have a strong, white body with a wing span that can reach up to a meter wide when in flight.
They have dark brown eyes surrounded by a ring of blue skin, distinctive feature among the white and yellow feathers.
The underwing and tail are tinged with pale yellow coloring.
They're often seen perched or hanging upside down on tree branches.
lorikeet: Lorikeets are known for their bright, vibrant plumage with multiple colors including green, blue, red, yellow and orange.
The body size of lorikeets is relatively small, typically between 7 and 12 inches long.
Lorikeets have a distinct pointed tail and slender body that can be distinguished from other bird species.
They possess small, rounded wings, perfect for quick, darting flight.
Lorikeets are identifiable by their curved beak and a tongue that is especially adapted for their nectar-based diet.
They have personality traits such as social, noisy, and very active, often seen hopping around and foraging.
Lorikeets have a unique feeding habit which can be used to identify them, they feed mainly on the nectar and pollen from flowers.
coucal: Coucals are typically large birds with a long tail which are part of the cuckoo family.
The particular species can often be identified by their distinct colorations, such as black, chestnut or dark green, along with white or buff underparts.
Coucals have a bulky body with a small head and thick, strong legs and feet that are used for walking and hopping on the ground.
They have a high-pitched, unique, cooing or bubbling call which can sometimes help in their identification.
They are often seen perched in trees or walking on the ground in search of food but are not very adept flyers.
They have a powerful, curved beak which is often used to catch their prey which includes various insects, small reptiles, and birds.
Coucals are often found in open grasslands, forests, and scrublands, and their larger size compared to other birds in these habitats can aid in their identification.
bee eater: Bee eaters are known for their vivid, multi-colored plumage, typically featuring a mix of yellows, greens, blues, and reds.
Bee eaters have elongated, pointed beaks that aid them in catching and eating insects, including bees and wasps.
The relative size of bee eaters is small to medium compared to other objects in the image.
Bee eaters possess a streamlined, slender body shape, ideal for agile flight and maneuverability.
They have a long, slender, and pointed tail. In some species, the tail ends in two elongated central feathers.
Their wings are pointed and can be broad or narrow, depending on the species.
They are often observed in flight, where their elegant gliding and swooping flight patterns are distinctive.
hornbill: These birds are characterized by a long, down-curved bill which is often brightly colored and comes with a casque (a hollow structure located on the bill).
Hornbills can vary greatly in size, ranging from the small Dwarf Hornbill measuring around 30 centimeters in length to the Great Hornbill which can reach up to 130 centimeters.
The relative size of hornbills is larger compared to other objects in the image.
Hornbills typically have broad wings and a long tail which helps them in flight.
Hornbills, particularly males, have very distinctive eyes, with the skin around the eyes often being a contrasting color to their plumage.
These birds are predominantly frugivorous, though they mix in insects and small animals into their diet.
Most Hornbill species are known for their unique and loud calls which can be heard for long distances.
hummingbird: Hummingbirds are small, colorful birds with iridescent feathers. Their colors can vary widely from green and blue to red, yellow, and orange.
Hummingbirds have a distinctive small, compact body shape compared to other birds.
One of the hallmarks of hummingbirds is their rapid wing movement. In a stationary photo, wings may appear blurred due to high-speed flapping.
Hummingbirds have a long and thin beak for probing deep into flowers for nectar, which is their primary food source.
The size of a hummingbird is relatively small, typically measuring between 3 to 5 inches in length.
Hummingbirds can often be seen hovering in the air at one spot. This behavior is quite unique among bird species.
Some species of hummingbirds feature a unique fan-shaped tail, while others have tapered tail feathers.
jacamar: Jacamars have bright, often iridescent colors, which can include tones of green, blue, and chestnut.
Jacamars have elongated bills and bodies, which aid in their lifestyle of catching insects in mid-air.
The size of a jacamar is relatively small compared to other objects present in the image.
Jacamars have feathered but slender and often rounded tails.
They have short and rounded wings because they are short-range flyers.
Jacamars are known for their perching habit, they usually perch upright on prominent bare twigs close to the canopy.
The eyes of a jacamar are dark in color, contributing to their distinctive facial appearance.
toucan: The most noticeable feature of a toucan is its large, colorful, and slightly curved beak. The colors can vary from yellow, green, red to black.
Toucans generally have black plumage with bright patches of color on their neck and chest. Some species may also have colored eye patches.
The tail of a toucan is usually red or a mix of red and black with a square or rounded end.
Toucans are known for their perching and hopping behavior on tree branches.
Size-wise, toucans are medium to large-sized birds, with bodies ranging from about 15 to 30 inches long, including the beak.
Toucans have two-toed feet which helps them to grip branches of trees.
A toucan's eyes are generally surrounded by brightly colored rings of skin, which can be blue, green, or red.
duck: Ducks generally have wide, flat bills that are adapted for filtering food from water. The color of the bill may vary, but it is often yellowish or orange.
Ducks have webbed feet, which are efficient for swimming. These are typically seen as three connected toes.
Ducks have a fairly distinct body shape - their bodies are usually broad and short, and they hold their tails upright.
Ducks are generally smaller than geese and swans, which are other members of the same bird family.
Ducks often display a variety of feather colors and patterns. Some male ducks, known as drakes, are usually more colorful than females.
Many ducks have a speculum - a band of color in their wing that is often iridescent and visible during flight.
Ducks are often seen near water bodies like ponds, lakes and rivers as they are aquatic birds.
red-breasted merganser: This bird species is known for their thin, sharp bills with serrated edges, designed for catching fish.
Males typically have a bold black and white pattern with a reddish-brown chest, while females have a gray body with a rusty head.
They are medium-sized diving ducks, characterized by their squat, streamlined bodies.
Their eyes are typically bright, with males displaying more striking colours than females.
They have a thoughtful and active behavior, often seen diving for fish or swiftly flying over the water's surface.
The relative size of red-breasted mergansers can help identify them, as they are generally larger than many other species of ducks.
This species is usually seen in coastal areas, near rivers, and large lakes.
goose: Geese are large birds, with size varying between species, but generally being bigger than ducks.
They typically have a long neck and stout body, with a wide wingspan which can make them appear larger than they actually are.
Geese have a broad, blunt-shaped beak which is often a lighter color or even orange, quite different from ducks.
Their plumage is usually white, gray or brown and some species like the Canada goose have distinct black heads and necks with a white chinstrap.
Geese have strong, webbed feet suitable for both land and water, much like other waterfowl.
Goose flight is heavily characterized by their distinctive V-formation, often seen during migration.
Geese are typically ground birds, meaning they spend a lot of time on land, often seen grazing on grass or other vegetation.
